title: The Palestinian flag in France: from student protests to social unrest | Al Majalla
text:
Amid the wave of demonstrations sweeping across France, one symbol has stood out amid the scenes of protest, violence, and vandalism: the Palestinian flag.
Since late September, students, trade unionists, and broad sections of French society have protested conditions in the country’s schools, the rising cost of living, and pressure on public services, culminating in a nationwide mobilisation on 17 October. The Interior Ministry estimated that about 550,000 people took part across France, including around 110,000 in Paris, while organisers put the national turnout at more than 800,000.
Against this backdrop, the Palestinian flag has emerged as a potent political symbol, invoked by different groups to mobilise crowds, express solidarity, and articulate political demands that extend beyond the Palestinian cause itself.
Yet the scenes unfolding across France, including the burning of a city hall in Limoges and peaceful student demonstrations in Paris, present two strikingly contrasting images: a student or academic draped in a keffiyeh on a university campus, and a Palestinian flag appearing amid scenes of looting and vandalism: two images, one flag.
The Palestinian flag has become a symbol for groups pursuing widely divergent objectives, with Palestinians themselves exercising little influence over its use or the meanings attached to it. How, then, did the Palestinian flag find its way into the streets of France?
A flag without borders
In the spring of 2024, the Palestinian flag became a prominent feature of France’s academic landscape. At Sciences Po in Paris, students waved Palestinian flags and wore keffiyehs, demanding that their institution take a stand against what the United Nations has termed an Israeli genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. The flag thereby became an instrument of protest. On 28 May that year, it crossed another threshold, moving from the university campus into the heart of France’s legislature when MP Sébastien Delogu raised it in the National Assembly, an act that led to his suspension.
Its presence spread to marches and trade union mobilisations. It acquired the capacity to connect causes separated by geography and political purpose, fulfilling a similar symbolic function in contexts that might otherwise have little in common.
The flag left Palestine, yet returned without bringing with it any of the political rights of the people it represents. The national emblem has acquired freedoms denied to its owners, as though it had rebelled against them, taking on an existence increasingly detached from the Palestinians themselves. The flag escaped the confines of a besieged homeland, crossed borders, found open doors, received refuge, and secured a place in the wider world. Meanwhile, Palestinians have struggled to access that same world.
The flag now appears at trade union demonstrations, on university campuses, in academic institutions, and in the highest political circles. It also appears amid scenes of vandalism and looting in the streets of France and elsewhere. A thief carries it, just as a student, an academic, a trade unionist, or a politician might. One emblem passes through different hands, serving divergent purposes and acquiring contradictory meanings. Even bitter adversaries may raise the same flag, each using it to tell a different story about their own cause and identity.
The French right invokes it to demonise demonstrations or portray protests and public discussions as threats to national identity and security, associating it with Islam, immigration, and cultural tensions. Israel, too, has seized on the flag's presence amid widespread social unrest across Europe, portraying the demonstrations as a breeding ground for antisemitism and pro-Palestinian militancy.
The left and parts of the political centre invoke it to mobilise supporters, rally public opinion, and champion political causes. Others seek to appropriate its moral authority to legitimise their rhetoric, demands, and presence in the public sphere.
Amid these competing appropriations, the flag circulates through a European political landscape over which Palestinians have no control. They cannot determine what it will signify when it appears, nor who will hold it.
Palestinians consequently find themselves expected to condemn the thief while thanking the student or academic who raises their flag. They watch the flag's original story recede behind the multitude of narratives that others seek to advance. They see it enlisted in struggles over identity, immigration, religion, and security. At the same time, their own story, like the Palestinians' collective national cause, fades into the background amid the growing politicisation of solidarity.
The flag has crossed borders that remain closed to Palestinians. It has entered universities and institutions while the people it represents lack the most basic conditions for education. It flies above demonstrations while those to whom it belongs are denied even the freedom to carry it in protest against killing, imprisonment, and siege.
